passages.t: Be strong and work, and the latter glory
passages.happening:
‘On the twenty-first day of the seventh month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet’ (verse 1). He is to ask the leaders and the people who among them saw this house in its former glory. ‘How does it look to you now? Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?’ (verse 3).

‘But now be strong, O Zerubbabel’, says the LORD, and be strong, Joshua, and all the people of the land: “Work! For I am with you” (verse 4). That was his promise when they came out of Egypt, ‘And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid’ (verse 5).

‘Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land’ (verse 6). He will shake all the nations, and they will come with their treasures, and he will fill this house with glory (verse 7). ‘The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts. The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the LORD of Hosts. And in this place I will provide peace’ (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
The date is about mid-October 520 BC, the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, Israel's autumn harvest festival, the same feast at which Solomon had dedicated the first temple. A thin harvest and a half-built temple made the contrast painful. Some of the oldest people could remember Solomon's temple before 587 BC, and the new foundations looked like nothing beside it.

God's answer has three parts: be strong and work; he is with them, as at the exodus; and the glory to come. Shaking the heavens and the earth was the language of God's coming at Sinai. The nations' treasures would come to the house, because the silver and gold were God's to give.
passages.later: Hebrews quotes verse 6: ‘Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well’ (Hebrews 12:26), and applies it to the final shaking that leaves a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Solomon dedicated the first temple at the same feast (1 Kings 8:2).
passages.hard:
How was the latter glory of this house greater than the former, when the second temple never matched Solomon's?

The difficulty is real. The second temple began small, lacked the ark of the covenant, and later tradition noted that no cloud of glory filled it at its dedication as it had filled Solomon's. Herod the Great began a vast rebuilding around 20 or 19 BC that made it one of the famous buildings of the Roman world, but that is not quite what Haggai promised either, and the temple was destroyed in AD 70.

Interpreters answer in several ways. Many Jewish and Christian readers take the promise as fulfilled in part by the wealth and honor the temple later drew from the nations, and look for its completion in the age to come. Christian interpreters have commonly seen the greater glory in the presence of Jesus in that temple. These notes leave the readings as readings.
passages.asks: The builders thought their work looked like nothing. Ask what small beginning you have despised in your own life or church. And God told them to be strong and work because he was with them. Ask what work he is asking you to keep doing.

passages.t: Holy and unclean, and from this day on
passages.happening:
On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, Haggai asks the priests for a ruling (verses 10-11). If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his robe and it touches other food, does that food become holy? ‘No,’ the priests answer (verse 12). If someone made unclean by touching a dead body touches any of it, does it become unclean? ‘Yes, it becomes defiled,’ they answer (verse 13). Haggai replies that so it is with this people and nation before God, ‘whatever they offer there is defiled’ (verse 14).

They are to consider their ways from this day. Before stone was laid on stone in the temple, a heap of twenty measures gave only ten, and fifty measures of wine only twenty (verses 15-16). God struck their work with blight, mildew and hail, but they did not turn to him (verse 17). Now, from the day the foundation was laid, though the seed is still in the barn and the trees have not borne fruit, ‘But from this day on, I will bless you’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The date is about mid-December 520 BC. The middle message turns on Israel's laws of holiness and impurity. Some things were holy, set apart to God, like the meat of a sacrifice; some were unclean, unfit for worship, like a person who had touched a dead body. The priests' task was to give rulings on such questions.

The answers make the point. Holiness does not pass on second hand, but uncleanness spreads easily. While the temple lay neglected, the people's offerings and work were made unclean by their neglect. Going on with sacrifices could not make them right with God.

Then the promise turns on a day. Nothing has grown yet; the seed is still in the barn. But from the day they laid the foundation, God promises good. The book's word about harvests belongs to that community and that covenant, not to a rule that hardship always means disobedience.
passages.later: The law made a person who touched a dead body unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), and gave the priests the work of teaching what was holy and what was common (Leviticus 10:10-11). Amos used the same refrain of warnings sent: blight and mildew, ‘yet you did not return to Me’ (Amos 4:9).
passages.asks: Holiness does not rub off, but neglect does. Ask whether you have been counting on religious activity to make up for a part of your life you have left undone. And God promised good from the day they began, before anything grew. Ask what you would begin today if you trusted that.

passages.happening:
On the same day the word of the LORD comes to Haggai a second time (verse 20). He is to tell Zerubbabel that God is about to shake the heavens and the earth (verse 21). He will overturn royal thrones and break the power of the kingdoms; chariots and riders will fall, each by his brother's sword (verse 22).

‘On that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will take you, My servant, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
A signet ring was a king's seal, pressed into clay or wax to mark documents with his authority. To be the king's signet ring was to carry his authority.

Zerubbabel was governor of a small Persian province, but he was also a descendant of David, a grandson of King Jehoiachin. Jeremiah had said of Jehoiachin, called Coniah, that even if he were a signet ring on God's right hand, God would pull him off. Haggai's promise reverses that judgment and keeps David's line alive.

No descendant of David reigned again as king, and after Zerubbabel the line disappears from public life. What remained was the promise. The overturning of thrones and chariots belongs to God's own shaking of the nations; it gives no one a warrant for violence in his name.
passages.later: Jeremiah had said of Jehoiachin, ‘even if you, Coniah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, were a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off’ (Jeremiah 22:24). Matthew and Luke both name Zerubbabel in the line of Jesus (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27).
passages.asks: God called a small-province governor his chosen signet ring. Ask what it means that God's promises often run through people who look unimportant. And ask whose authority you carry in the way you live.
